procedural_history.impugned_order: Remand order dated August 1970 remanding the petitioner to jail custody.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: The petitioner filed a writ petition No. 315 of 1970 for Habeas Corpus challenging his detention.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The petitioner filed a Writ Petition No. 330 of 1970 in the Supreme Court under Article 32 of the Constitution of India for a writ in the nature of habeas corpus, praying for immediate release on the ground that the remand order was illegal.

directions: The orders of remand dated 28th and 29th August, 1970 passed by the City Magistrate, Lucknow are illegal.
The detention of the petitioner in the Central Jail, New Delhi, after the midnight of August 28, 1970 on the authority of the illegal orders of remand is also illegal.
The petitioner should be set at liberty forthwith.

issue.issue_text: Whether the physical production of a person before a magistrate is an essential prerequisite for the magistrate to pass a valid order of remand into custody.

law.law_text: The various provisions of the Criminal Procedure Code require that authorities seeking to curtail the liberty of a subject must strictly and scrupulously observe the forms and rules of the law.

The dissenting judges and previous court decisions held that an order of remand passed without the accused being produced is illegal, as it prevents the accused from making representations and risks magistrates passing orders mechanically.

application.application_text: The majority of the Court held that while it is desirable for a magistrate to have the prisoner produced before them when remitting them to further custody, it is not an absolute or essential requirement.

The Court reasoned that a magistrate must be able to act as the circumstances permit. It provided a specific example to illustrate this point: if an accused person is so seriously ill that they cannot be brought to court, a trial may need to be adjourned and a remand order issued in their absence. The Court stated that such an order, made without the production of the accused, would not be invalid.

reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court concluded that a magistrate can pass a valid order of remand into custody even without the physical production of the accused. The Court reasoned that while production is desirable, a magistrate can act as circumstances permit, such as when an accused is too ill to be brought to court. Therefore, physical production is not an essential prerequisite for a valid remand order.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the physical production of a person before a magistrate is an essential prerequisite for the magistrate to pass a valid order of remand into custody.
appellant_arguments: The petitioner argued that their detention was illegal because the remand orders were not passed according to law, implying that their physical absence before the magistrate at the time of remand invalidated the order.
respondent_arguments: The City Magistrate (respondent) contended that the proceedings were legal and valid. They justified passing the remand order in the petitioner's absence by explaining that the petitioner had been brought to New Delhi under the Supreme Court's orders, making physical production before the magistrate in Lucknow impractical or impossible.

cases.principle: Authorities seeking to curtail the liberty of a subject must strictly and scrupulously observe the forms and rules of the law.
An order of remand passed without the accused being produced is illegal.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: An order of remand passed by a magistrate is illegal if the accused is not physically produced before the court when the order is made.
obiter: Authorities seeking to curtail the liberty of a subject must strictly and scrupulously observe the forms and rules of the law.
When a prisoner under trial is in the custody of the Supreme Court, a magistrate can extend the remand by intimating the relevant parties without the prisoner's physical presence.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The various provisions of the Criminal Procedure Code, referred to by us, as also the decisions quoted above lead to the conclusion that the accused must be present before the magistrate or court when an order of remand is passed. In fact the decisions quoted by us clearly lay down that an order of remand passed without the accused being produced, is i!legal. We rue in agreement with those decisions.
legal_tests_applied: This Court has often reiterated before that those who feel called upoa to deprive other persons of their personal liberty in the discharge of what they conceive to be their duty, must strictly and scrupulously observe the forms and rules of the law.
policy_considerations: When the personal liberty of a person is sought to be restricted or curtailed, rules of the law as well as the forms must be scruplously observed.
